sn47.7:1.4: Folklore is replete with stories of fools getting stuck in tar. Ja 55 tells of a warrior whose five weapons serve only to stick him to the coat of a _yakkha_. The Phillipine folk-tale Masoy and the Ape tells of an ape getting stuck in tar in the shape of a man. These are examples of “The Tarbaby and the Rabbit” story type. The current case is a little different, as there is no doll or mannikin. Rather, according to the commentary, the tar (_lepa_)—which was made from the sap from the banyan tree—was smeared on the trees and branches where monkeys went.
sn47.7:2.13: In his note on this Sutta, Bodhi acknowledges the difficult reading _kaṭṭha-kataṅgāre_ and proposes the emendation _kaliṅgare_ (“log, piece of wood”) based on the Buddhist Sanskrit _kāṣṭha-kaḍambara_. He then takes it to mean a block of wood, to which the hunter fastens the monkey before leaving with both monkey and block. This, however, creates several problems. Since both _kaṭṭha_ and _kaliṅgara_ mean “block of wood”, why the compound? Why does the hunter need to secure the monkey to the wood, when the whole point of the simile was that the monkey was stuck? Why read the verb _avassajjetvā_ as “having fastened” when ithe normal meaning of _avassajati_ is “release”, confirmed by the BJT reading _uddharitvā_? And why would the hunter return from remote regions carrying a log of wood? I agree that the text is probably corrupt_kaṭṭhakaliṅgara_. However I am puzzled at why he renders avassajjati as “fastens”, saying this “follows the verb”. I’m not aware of any context where this verb means that. In fact, avassajjati/ossajjati (and its many variant spellings) means to opposite: to release, send off, etc. Why would the hunter walk off carrying the block of tarred wood? Surely it means that he released the monkey from the wood, thus achieving what the monkey could not. A similar sense is associated with yena kamam pakkamati at AN 5.75.
